links.caveat: The mode peaks in spring and the Sahel's rains come in July– September; the arrow assumes the contrast lasts into summer, which it does in some years and not others. The Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean also move the Sahel's rains, and the decades-long swings belong to the AMO's arrow rather than this one.
links.evidence_note: Wet Sahel years go with a warm north and a cool south tropical Atlantic and a rain belt displaced north; over the drought decades the north Atlantic cooled, the south warmed and the wind confluence over the eastern Atlantic moved 150–200 km south, most of all in July–August, enough to account for the fall in Sahel rain; the studies work with the sea-temperature pattern rather than the spring mode itself.

links.mechanism: With the north Atlantic cool and the south warm, the rain belt over the eastern Atlantic and West Africa sits further south in summer, and the monsoon's rains fall short of the Sahel.
links.caveat: Same limits as the wet side: the spring contrast has to last into summer, and the Sahel answers other oceans too. The long drought of the 1970s and 1980s was the AMO's cool decades, not a run of single springs.
links.evidence_note: Dry Sahel years go with a cool north and a warm south tropical Atlantic and a rain belt displaced south; the drought decades show the same pattern in every season, strongest in boreal summer.

links.mechanism: A warm tropical North Atlantic keeps the rain belt and the rising air north of the equator through the southern winter. The trade winds that would carry Atlantic moisture into the southern Amazon weaken, the air over the region sinks, and the dry season runs long and hot.
links.caveat: Known from two droughts, 2005 and 2010, and a short record of correlations, so shown as probable. El Niño dries the Amazon too, but in the wet season and on the northern side of the basin, which is why the map keeps the two regions apart. How much the drought costs depends on the fires people set.
links.evidence_note: The 2005 drought of southwestern Amazonia was not related to El Niño but to the anomalously warm tropical North Atlantic, weaker trade-wind moisture transport into southern Amazonia and weakened rising motion, intensified through the dry season into September; the Atlantic influence over 1979–2005 is comparable to the Pacific's and falls in the dry season; the 2010 drought was intensified by the same warming of the tropical North Atlantic through a longer dry season.

links.mechanism: With the tropical North Atlantic cool and the rain belt sitting south, the trade winds are proposed to carry more moisture into the southern Amazon, so the dry season is milder and the rivers stay higher.
links.caveat: The wet side is an inference from the correlation and the mechanism: the studies are about the two droughts, and there is no well-studied case of a cool north Atlantic spring giving the southern Amazon a gentle dry season. Shown as contested for that reason.
links.evidence_note: The analysis of 1979–2005 finds a linear Atlantic influence on Amazon dry-season rainfall, which would run both ways, but the papers document the dry years only.

links.mechanism: A warm tropical North Atlantic and Caribbean gives the tropical waves that cross it in early summer more moisture and energy, so the first half of the rainy season, from May to July, tends to be wetter over the Caribbean and Central America.
links.caveat: The early season answers the Atlantic; the late season, from August, answers the Pacific, and an El Niño can cancel the wet tendency. The studies use the north Atlantic's temperature rather than the spring mode itself, and the rain belt's position matters more for the Pacific coast of Central America than for the islands.
links.evidence_note: Early-season (May–July) Caribbean rainfall is strongly influenced by warm water in the tropical North Atlantic between the equator and 20°N, the band where tropical waves develop, while the late season answers the equatorial Pacific and Atlantic; Central America is wettest when the north Atlantic is warm and the eastern Pacific cool.

links.mechanism: An El Niño winter weakens the northeast trade winds over the tropical Atlantic through the same chain of high and low pressure that reaches North America. Weaker trades mean less evaporation and less cooling, so the northern tropical Atlantic warms in late winter and the contrast with the south peaks the following spring.
links.caveat: The warming trails the El Niño's peak by four to five months, so from a June start it arrives the following March and most of the mode's own effects fall after the year shown. Not every El Niño warms the Atlantic; a positive NAO winter can undo it.
links.evidence_note: Half to four fifths of the north Atlantic trade-wind belt's temperature variability goes with the Pacific ENSO, with Atlantic warmings four to five months after the mature phase of Pacific warm events, through reduced trade winds and reduced evaporative cooling, best developed in the spring after; almost all extreme north tropical Atlantic springs since 1950 relate to ENSO or the NAO; the mode's spring predictability comes from the tropical Pacific.

links.mechanism: A La Niña winter strengthens the northeast trades over the tropical Atlantic, more evaporation cools the northern side, and the contrast tips the other way the following spring.
links.caveat: The Atlantic's answer to a La Niña is weaker and less regular than its answer to an El Niño, and the study that found the lag looked at warm events; shown one tier lower for that reason.
links.evidence_note: The remote-forcing study finds that the north tropical Atlantic's extreme springs of both signs relate to ENSO or the NAO through the trade winds and evaporation; the lag analysis itself was done on Pacific warm events.

links.mechanism: A negative NAO winter weakens the Azores high and with it the northeast trade winds. Weaker trades evaporate less water from the northern tropical Atlantic, which warms through late winter, and wind and evaporation then feed on each other to hold the warm north through spring.
links.caveat: The NAO changes from month to month, so a single stormy December may not be enough; it is a winter's average that matters. The link is drawn from the NAO as chosen in December; the mode's own summer effects then fall inside the year shown, which is the point of the chain.
links.evidence_note: Almost all extreme north tropical Atlantic springs since 1950 relate to either ENSO or the NAO, which lead them, through changes in surface winds and evaporation; the spring meridional modes are forced by trade-wind variations in the northern subtropical ocean; the 2009 negative event began with a stronger subtropical high and stronger trades in January–February, the mirror case.

links.mechanism: A positive NAO winter strengthens the Azores high and the northeast trades, more evaporation cools the northern tropical Atlantic, and the contrast tips negative in spring, with the rain belt held south.
links.caveat: Same limits as the mirror link: a winter's average matters, not one month, and an El Niño in the same winter works the other way.
links.evidence_note: The strong negative event of 2009 was initiated by stronger than normal trade winds in January and February with a strengthened subtropical North Atlantic high, cooling the ocean by evaporation and deepening the mixed layer; the remote-forcing study ties such springs to the NAO and ENSO.

links.mechanism: Warm water off Baja California weakens the trade winds to its south, the weaker wind evaporates less and warms the sea further, and the warm patch and the weak wind creep south-west together through spring. By summer the weak wind reaches the equator, where it lets warm water spread east and starts the Pacific toward an El Niño by the following winter.
links.caveat: A nudge, not a trigger: the Pacific has to be primed, with heat already stored in the west, for the spring signal to grow, and about one positive spring in three comes to nothing. The spring of 2014 was one such miss. Part of the mode is also El Niño's own footprint in the subtropics, so the two are not fully separate things.
links.evidence_note: The majority of El Niño events over four decades were preceded by the mode's spring warming and south-westerly wind; in a high-resolution coupled model it acts as a trigger seven to nine months before large El Niños, but not every event triggers one and the western Pacific has to be preconditioned; imposing the winter forcing in a coupled model warmed the ENSO region in about 70% of sixty runs; positive springs forecast eastern Pacific El Niños with some skill in a multi-model hindcast; the spring-to-winter relation has strengthened over the past seventy years.

links.mechanism: Cool water off Baja California and stronger trades are proposed to work the mirror way: the stronger wind cools the sea further, the pattern creeps toward the equator, and by summer the stronger easterlies there lift cool water in the east and start the Pacific toward a La Niña.
links.caveat: The negative side is the weak side. In the observed record negative springs are poor predictors of La Niña, and the studies that made the case for the mode are about the positive springs before El Niños. Shown as contested for that reason; the map draws it so the asymmetry can be seen, not because it is reliable.
links.evidence_note: In the multi-model hindcast negative mode events poorly predict La Niña events in observations, and the forecast models fail to capture even that; the subtropical route into ENSO produces multi-year La Niñas but not multi-year El Niños, one source of the asymmetry between the two.

links.mechanism: Rain rising over the warm water of the mode's north-western arm sets up a wave-like response to its west: low-level westerly winds and a spin over the south-eastern part of the typhoon breeding grounds, and weaker wind shear aloft. Typhoons form further east and have a longer run over warm water to grow.
links.caveat: The count is a tendency, not a forecast, and one study finds the year-to-year part of the relation weak once the slow decadal swing of the tropical Pacific is removed; the model experiments that back the link are what keep it at probable. Its effect adds to El Niño's own, which points the same way.
links.evidence_note: A positive mode favours typhoon formation in the western North Pacific and a negative one inhibits it, in observations, a thousand-year control run and sensitivity experiments, through the wind shear over the south-eastern breeding grounds; the mode index correlates with the number of intense typhoons in June–November; the summer of 2018, with no El Niño, had eighteen typhoons and sensitivity runs put the positive mode as the main cause; in 2015 the mode's warm water pushed the mean birthplace of typhoons ten degrees east of 1997's. One study finds the statistical link is dominated by decadal covariation with the tropical Pacific.

links.mechanism: With the subtropical north-east Pacific cool, the wave-like response over the typhoon grounds runs the other way: stronger wind shear and less spin over the south-eastern breeding grounds, so typhoons form closer to Asia and stay weaker.
links.caveat: The composite study finds the quiet tendency, but the case studies and the model experiments are about positive springs, and the objection that the year-to-year relation is weak applies with more force here. Shown one tier lower than the warm side for that reason.
links.evidence_note: The negative phase inhibits typhoon occurrence in the western North Pacific in the composite analysis of observations and the control run; the one-in-ten-years component of the relation, rather than the year-to-year one, carries most of the signal.

links.mechanism: The mode's warm water lies over the western part of the eastern Pacific hurricane grounds, between Mexico and Hawaii. Warm sea, moist air and weak wind shear there give storms more fuel and more room, and more of them travel west toward Hawaii.
links.caveat: Rests on one season, 2015, and its model experiments, and that season had a strong El Niño at the same time; the record of storms in this basin is short. Shown as contested until more seasons are studied.
links.evidence_note: The record 2015 season in the eastern and central Pacific, with the first three simultaneous category-4 hurricanes and a record count around Hawaii, was not primarily caused by the El Niño but by warm water in the subtropical Pacific typical of the positive mode, according to targeted high-resolution experiments; the western part of the basin set records for storms, hurricane days and storm energy in 2015, with the El Niño and the positive mode together giving a record-warm background.

links.mechanism: The haze of sulphuric-acid droplets in the stratosphere reflects a few per cent of incoming sunlight back to space. Less sunlight reaches the surface, the land and the upper ocean lose more heat than they gain, and the world's average temperature drops by a few tenths of a degree, most in the first summer after the eruption, then creeps back over two or three years as the haze settles out.
links.caveat: The dip is small next to a strong El Niño or the warming trend, and is easiest to see once El Niño's own warmth is taken out of the record. The map cannot weigh a cooling volcano against a warming El Niño: when both point at this region it shows a disagreement, as in 1992, when in reality the volcano won and the world cooled despite the El Niño.
links.evidence_note: A climate-model forecast made within months of Pinatubo predicted cooling from late 1991 peaking in late 1992, large enough to overwhelm the developing El Niño's warmth; observed global temperatures fell by up to half a degree by mid-1992, and satellite lower-troposphere temperatures by half a degree by September 1992; a composite of five major tropical eruptions shows significant cooling once ENSO is removed; ten reanalyses agree on tropical cooling after most but not all eruptions; the observed drying of the air amplified the cooling, which a model could not reproduce without water-vapour feedback.

links.mechanism: A cooler surface evaporates less, so there is less water in the air to rain out, and the land cools faster than the sea, which weakens the contrast that draws the summer monsoon inland. If the haze sits more in the northern hemisphere, as most tropical clouds do, the tropical rain belt also shifts south, away from the Sahel.
links.caveat: Comes mostly from models and a handful of twentieth-century eruptions; in the observed record the summer signal is only marginally detectable, and the sign depends on which hemisphere gets more haze: a cloud that stays south of the equator can leave the Sahel wetter. The high-latitude eruptions that dried the Sahel most, Laki in 1783 among them, are not on this map. For a June eruption the next Sahel rains fall in the month after the year shown, so the arrow stays waiting.
links.evidence_note: Global and monsoon rainfall drop after eruptions in CMIP5 models and in three observational datasets, with the rain belt shifting away from the hemisphere holding more aerosol; land precipitation and river runoff fell to record lows in the year after Pinatubo once ENSO is accounted for; a hemispherically lopsided haze shifts Sahelian rainfall, with northern-hemisphere loading drying the Sahel in a model and in the record; most CMIP5 models show clear reductions of summer monsoon rainfall in the first year after large eruptions since 1850; the warm-season influence is only marginally detectable in the observations; a model of the 1783 Laki eruption dried the Sahel by one to three millimetres a day and cut the flow of the Nile.

links.mechanism: The monsoon is driven by the summer contrast between hot land and cooler sea. Under the haze the land cools faster than the ocean, the contrast weakens, and a cooler atmosphere holds less water, so the first monsoon after the haze has spread tends to bring less rain.
links.caveat: Most of the evidence is from models. The tree-ring record of monsoon Asia shows drier central Asia but wetter mainland south-east Asia in eruption years, which the models do not reproduce, and India's own monsoon of 1992 was only modestly below normal. Both the eruption and any El Niño it may favour point the same way, so the two are hard to separate in the record.
links.evidence_note: Monsoon rainfall decreases after eruptions in CMIP5 models and in observations; most CMIP5 models show clear reductions of summer monsoon rainfall in the first year after large eruptions; in a last-millennium ensemble northern-hemisphere cooling shifts the rain belt toward the equator and suppresses the south-east Asian monsoon even without an El Niño; drought reconstructions find drier central Asia but wetter mainland south-east Asia in eruption years, so models may miss part of the response; large eruptions strengthen the coupling between ENSO and the Indian monsoon in a model and in a millennium of records; land rainfall and runoff fell to record lows in the year after Pinatubo.

links.mechanism: The haze absorbs some sunlight and warms the stratosphere over the tropics more than over the pole. The sharper contrast strengthens the winter polar vortex, the jet beneath it shifts north, and mild Atlantic air is carried deep into northern Europe in the first winter after the eruption, outweighing the cooling from lost sunlight. This is the "winter warming" of a cool volcanic year.
links.caveat: The observed pattern is an average over a dozen eruptions and a single winter can go either way; models produce it weakly if at all, and one study argues the mild winter of 1991–92 after Pinatubo was probably chance, or the El Niño's doing, rather than the volcano's. Second winters show little of it, and the map's season gate cannot tell a first winter from a second.
links.evidence_note: The twelve largest eruptions of 1883–1992 were followed by winter warming over Eurasia and North America significant at the 95% level, in the first winter for tropical eruptions; the same pattern follows fifteen tropical eruptions in half a millennium of European reconstructions, with a positive NAO; four centuries of records give a mean response resembling the Arctic Oscillation but a spread larger than the mean; the winter warming after Pinatubo is reproduced in one model and much more weakly than observed or not at all in the IPCC AR4 and CMIP5 ensembles, though most CMIP5 models show it when only the first winter is examined; large ensembles find the effect tiny next to winter-to-winter variability, and the 1991–92 warming is reproduced in one model only with the observed El Niño sea-surface temperatures specified; all datasets in a ten-reanalysis comparison show the warm anomaly over northern Europe.

links.mechanism: The same strengthened winter vortex and stronger westerlies that warm northern Europe reach furthest east over Russia and Siberia, the core of the winter-warming pattern, where the first winter after a tropical eruption tends to be milder than usual even while the planet as a whole is cooler.
links.caveat: The same evidence as for northern Europe, with the same doubts: a tendency averaged over a dozen eruptions, weak in most models, and possibly chance in the one winter, 1991–92, that everyone remembers. The map cannot tell a first winter from a second, and the second shows little of it.
links.evidence_note: Warming over Eurasia after the twelve largest eruptions since 1883, in the first winter after tropical ones; warm anomalies throughout northern Eurasia in four centuries of cold-season reconstructions and in model simulations of them; observed January circulation changes after three eruptions explained by stationary-wave changes under a strengthened polar-night jet; CMIP5 models fail to capture the Eurasian warming when two winters are combined but most show it in the first winter alone; the effect is tiny against internal variability in large ensembles.

links.mechanism: Heating of the tropical stratosphere by the haze strengthens the winter polar vortex, and a strong vortex reaches down to the surface as a positive North Atlantic Oscillation: the Iceland low deeper, the Azores high stronger, the westerlies across the Atlantic stronger and further north.
links.caveat: Found in the pressure record after most large eruptions but, in the words of one review of ten reanalyses, not as clear cut as the literature suggests: the spread between eruptions is large, models make the vortex response small, and the polar response turns out not to be a direct effect of the heating but to go through stratospheric wave activity, sensitive to the shape of the cloud. Drawn dashed for that reason; with the chain on, the NAO's own winter arrows follow one tier down.
links.evidence_note: Both the Arctic Oscillation and the NAO are excited in the first winter after thirteen major eruptions since 1870, significant at 95%, the signal larger for the NAO; the winter response to fifteen tropical eruptions in European reconstructions follows a positive NAO; four centuries of records give a mean response resembling the Arctic Oscillation; ten reanalyses and the Hadley Centre pressure record confirm a positive NAO tendency in the winters after large eruptions, with a large spread for individual eruptions; AR4 models simulate a positive Arctic Oscillation but with far weaker surface effects, and CMIP5 models generally fail to capture the strengthened vortex and positive NAO; in one Earth-system model the vortex response is insignificant for observation-based forcings and depends on the structure of the aerosol cloud.

links.mechanism: Two routes are proposed. The haze cools land faster than sea, and cooling over tropical Africa weakens the West African monsoon and sends a wave of westerly wind along the equator that reaches the western Pacific and lets warm water spread east. And in the eastern Pacific the cold water welling up from below is cooled less than the surface around it, so the west cools more than the east, the trade winds slacken, and the Pacific drifts toward El Niño in the year after the eruption.
links.caveat: Genuinely unsettled. Coral and tree-ring records and CMIP5 composites lean toward an El Niño in the year after big tropical eruptions, but a thousand years of central-Pacific coral finds no significant response, one model starts with a La Niña before any El Niño, and the answer depends on the season of the eruption and on what the Pacific was already doing: an eruption in a La Niña year does little. Pinatubo's own El Niño was already under way when it erupted, so 1991 cannot settle the question.
links.evidence_note: Proxy records show an El Niño-like response to volcanic forcing over the past several centuries; in an intermediate model only eruptions larger than Pinatubo shift El Niño likelihood above internal variability, and volcanism raises the odds by about half on average rather than triggering events; CMIP5 shows an El Niño tending to peak in the year after large eruptions, with targeted simulations tracing it to cooling over tropical Africa; 122 CMIP5 members show co-occurring El Niño and positive Indian Ocean Dipole events peaking six to twelve months after the forcing peaks; a Pinatubo-size eruption produces a significant El Niño response a year on in one coupled model except when the Pacific starts in La Niña, and more strongly for summer eruptions; another coupled model gives an El Niño-like warming a year after the peak forcing, and the eruption season matters for the eruption-year response; against it, fossil corals from the central Pacific show only a weak, insignificant El Niño-like tendency over the last millennium, and one coupled model's first response is La Niña-like.

links.mechanism: In an El Niño winter the air over the Indian Ocean and the western Pacific sinks and pressure there rises. Around the northwest edge of that high, winds tend to blow from the Arabian Sea and tropical Africa toward Iran and Afghanistan, feeding the winter storms that cross from the Mediterranean with extra moisture, so they drop more rain and mountain snow.
links.caveat: The signal is strongest in autumn and spring and patchier in midwinter, and it varies from place to place: parts of Iran show it clearly, others hardly at all. A model ensemble gives an El Niño cold season roughly even odds of landing in the wettest third and a one-in-four chance of landing in the driest, so a wet season is a lean, not a promise. The connection has strengthened in recent decades and may not hold in every era.
links.evidence_note: Observed precipitation, moisture flux and pressure data and an atmospheric model agree on extra southwesterly moisture into the region in warm ENSO events, greatest in the transition seasons; Iranian station rainfall in El Niño autumns was several times that of La Niña autumns over 1951–1990; seasonal November–April precipitation over southwest Asia correlates with ENSO and Pacific decadal patterns; a regional climate model reproduces the observed increase in the warm ENSO phase over northern Pakistan, Afghanistan and Tajikistan through stronger western disturbances; an ensemble forced with 1979–2015 conditions puts above-average precipitation in both El Niño types, with the spread between members nearly as large as the mean shift.

links.mechanism: In a La Niña winter the rising air and heavy rain sit over the warm pool of the western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean. That rain sends a wave through the atmosphere that strengthens sinking air over Iran and Afghanistan and steers moisture away, so the winter storms arrive dry or not at all.
links.caveat: The drying is clearest when La Niña comes with an unusually warm western Pacific, as in 1998–2001; a La Niña centred in the eastern Pacific barely shifts the odds in one model ensemble. Two or three years of La Niña do far more harm than one, because reservoirs and soils run down, and the famine of 2000–2001 owed as much to war as to weather.
links.evidence_note: The 1998–2001 drought that affected sixty million people fell in a prolonged La Niña with warm western-Pacific waters, and cold-season precipitation over the region varies opposite to rainfall over the eastern Indian Ocean; a study of recent warm-west-Pacific La Niñas traces Northern Hemisphere drought, southwest Asia included, to the same forcing; central-Pacific La Niñas push the region's November–April precipitation into the driest third more than seven times in ten in an ensemble, while eastern-Pacific La Niñas do not change the odds; the observational analysis behind the El Niño link finds the reverse pattern in cold events.

links.mechanism: With cold water on the equator and the tropical rain belt pushed north, a wave of high pressure tends to set up over the central United States in late spring and the jet stream, with its storms, is displaced far north into Canada. Moist Gulf air still flows north but little of it is lifted into rain, and the soil dries out, which feeds the heat and the drought.
links.caveat: Summer links are weaker and less reliable than ENSO's winter ones, and this one has switched on and off over the last century: it was strong from 1948 to 1978 and hard to find from 1979 on, depending on what the North Pacific was doing. Not every La Niña summer is dry, and the 1988 drought had begun on the West Coast a year earlier for other reasons. The map holds the phase for the year, so the following summer is shaded too; the evidence is for the summer the event is in.
links.evidence_note: Record low April–June 1988 rainfall in the north-central United States followed a wave train from the tropical Pacific that a planetary-wave model reproduces from the displaced rain belt over cold equatorial water; in 1988 the jet and storm track were the furthest north of any year from 1979 to 1993; model composites put ENSO's drought influence over the Great Plains with cold events favouring drought; the central-US summer teleconnection was active in 1871–1916 and 1948–78 and absent in 1917–47 and after 1979.

links.mechanism: Warm water on the equator shifts the tropical rain belt and the heating of the atmosphere, and the jet stream over North America tends to sit further south than usual for the season, in a springlike position across the central United States. Storms then run along it over the Midwest, lifting Gulf moisture into repeated heavy rain.
links.caveat: Genuinely unsettled. The 1993 flood summer fits, and one analysis of 1950–1990 finds Great Plains summer rain rising with warm tropical Pacific water, but the same teleconnection was absent for decades at a time, and over the central-eastern United States ENSO's summer and winter effects run opposite and cancel. Most El Niños begin in spring or summer and their summer effects are much weaker than the winter ones. The map holds the phase for the year, so the following summer is shaded too.
links.evidence_note: The 1993 floods came with a mature El Niño, a broader jet stream and storm track displaced well south of normal, the furthest south by over 200 km of any year from 1979 to 1993; Great Plains summer precipitation over 1950–1990 covaries with El Niño–La Niña water in the tropical Pacific; model composites give warm events a wet-spell tendency over the Plains; against it, the central-US summer teleconnection was absent in 1917–47 and after 1979, and drought and wet spells over the central-eastern United States are short because ENSO's summer and winter effects there oppose each other.

links.mechanism: A positive North Atlantic Oscillation deepens the Icelandic low. The winds on its western side blow from the north across Baffin Island, Labrador and Hudson Bay, pulling Arctic air south while Europe on the eastern side gets the mild westerlies. It is the same see-saw that makes Greenland cold when Europe is warm.
links.caveat: Strongest toward Labrador and Baffin Island and weaker on the west side of Hudson Bay, where ENSO and the Pacific matter more. The oscillation swings from week to week, so a positive winter on average still has mild spells; and the winter of 2009–10, with the most negative index on record, still froze the region.
links.evidence_note: The positive winters of the 1980s and early 1990s brought cold conditions to the northwest Atlantic while Europe warmed; the NAO is the dominant mode for Canadian winter temperature, its effect confined mainly to the northeast of the country; high-index winters show more frequent and longer cold spells over eastern Canada; decadal swings of the oscillation are mirrored in temperatures over Greenland and eastern Canada.

links.mechanism: With the Icelandic low weak and the Azores high feeble, the flow of Arctic air down the Labrador coast slackens. Milder Atlantic air reaches Hudson Bay and the northeast, blocking highs over Greenland hold it there, and the cold spills into Europe instead. Winter sea ice on the bay and along Labrador tends to form late and thin.
links.caveat: As for the positive phase: clearest toward the Labrador coast, and a negative winter is mild on average, not every week. The mildness arrives as the phase does, with no lag, and it ends when the phase ends, which the map cannot show. Where El Niño is also pushing the region mild the two cannot be told apart on the map.
links.evidence_note: Regressions of winter temperature on the NAO index reverse sign between Europe and the northwest Atlantic, so the negative phase warms Labrador and eastern Canada as the positive cools it; the NAO explains more of northeastern Canada's winter temperature variance than ENSO or the PDO; low-index winters bring fewer cold spells over eastern Canada.

links.mechanism: The heating of the air over the warm eastern Pacific launches the wave train across North America that lifts the jet stream north over western Canada. Mild Pacific air follows it, and in most El Niño winters the warmth spreads east across southern Canada, reaching Hudson Bay as a weaker version of the Prairie signal.
links.caveat: The warmth fades eastward and studies disagree about whether it reaches the northeast at all: one composite finds El Niño winters warm over most of Canada, another finds the east warm only when the Pacific Decadal Oscillation is also positive and cool when it is neutral. The North Atlantic Oscillation matters more here, and in a winter when it is positive its cold tends to win.
links.evidence_note: A canonical correlation analysis of Canadian temperatures finds El Niño winters warm over most of the country, weakening eastward; most of southern Canada sees mean winter temperature shifted to warmer values in El Niño; El Niño winters have more warm spells and fewer cold spells across most of Canada; against it, the ENSO effect on winter temperature is mainly over western and central Canada, and in El Niño winters with a neutral PDO the east is cooler than normal.

links.mechanism: Cold water on the equator weakens the wave train that steers the jet stream north, so Arctic air spills south across Canada more often. The cooling is strongest on the Prairies and reaches the northeast weakly, and more often through Arctic outbreaks than through a steady cold.
links.caveat: Weaker and less consistent than the El Niño warming and, like it, strongest in the west. The eastern response depends on what the North Pacific and the North Atlantic are doing in the same winter, and one composite finds the eastern cooling small. Treat the map's cold as a lean, and look at the NAO first.
links.evidence_note: La Niña winters are cold over most of Canada in the canonical correlation analysis, weaker in the east; La Niña winters show more cold spells and fewer warm spells across most of the country; the regression analysis finds the ENSO influence confined mainly to western and central Canada.

links.mechanism: An El Niño peaks in winter and its warmth spreads through the tropics over the following months: the air over India is warmer, the winter rains that moisten the soil of the north are often short, and a persistent high with clear skies and dry ground sets up over central and northwestern India in the spring after the event, the ingredients of a heat wave.
links.caveat: Unsettled. Composites of El Niño years are warmer in the following pre-monsoon season, but not significantly so over large areas; the significant warmth is in the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons of the event year, which this node does not show. One study ties one type of Indian heat wave to cooling in the Pacific, the opposite sign, and another to blocking over the North Atlantic, with no Pacific link at all. The warming trend has added more to India's heat waves than any El Niño.
links.evidence_note: Heat waves over India during 1961–2013 vary with central Pacific and tropical Indian Ocean temperatures, with more frequent El Niños expected to lengthen them; composites over 1901–2007 show El Niño years warm through the monsoon, post-monsoon and the following winter and pre-monsoon, significant only in the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons; against it, one of two heat-wave types over coastal eastern India is tied to anomalous cooling in the Pacific, and the other over north-central India to North Atlantic blocking.

links.mechanism: A La Niña cools the tropics as an El Niño warms them, and the cooling lingers into the following spring. With a cooler atmosphere and fewer persistent highs over the north, the pre-monsoon tends to run less hot and heat waves tend to be fewer and shorter.
links.caveat: Unsettled, and thinner than the El Niño side: the cool composite is the mirror image of a warm one that is itself not significant in this season, and one analysis links heat waves along India's east coast to Pacific cooling, which would make a La Niña spring hotter there, not cooler. No La Niña spring is safe from heat: 2022's March heat came in a La Niña.
links.evidence_note: Composites of La Niña years over 1901–2007 are close to the mirror of El Niño's, with negative temperature anomalies persisting from the event's monsoon season to the following pre-monsoon; against it, heat waves over coastal eastern India are associated with anomalous cooling in the Pacific through a weakened sea breeze.

links.mechanism: A warm Indian Ocean warms the air above it and the moist air flowing onto India from the south. It also weakens the contrast between the land and the sea that drives the sea breezes along the coast, so the coast gets less relief, and the whole subcontinent starts the hot season from a higher floor.
links.caveat: One study's finding, on a short record, and hard to separate from El Niño because the basin warms after one: the springs of 1998, 2010 and 2016 had both. The basin-wide warming trend of recent decades is bound up with the same statistic. Treat this as one more reason a post-El Niño spring runs hot, not as an independent forecast.
links.evidence_note: The variability of heat waves over India during 1961–2013 is influenced by tropical Indian Ocean as well as central Pacific temperatures, and warming of the tropical Indian Ocean is expected to bring more frequent and longer heat waves.

links.mechanism: Two routes are proposed. Rain over the central Pacific in an El Niño winter launches waves along the jet stream that cross North America, the Atlantic and North Africa and arrive over the Himalaya, where they favour rising air and snowfall. And the suppressed rain over the western Pacific sets up a cyclonic swirl that pulls cold air and tropical moisture onto the eastern plateau, where both cool the ground and thicken the snow.
links.caveat: Contested and built on a short satellite snow record. The proposed wave path is a speculation supported by ray tracing; the two studies that find more snow disagree about where on the plateau it falls; and the relationship between ENSO and spring snow cover changed sign in the early 2000s, positive before and negative after. Some studies find the plateau's snow independent of ENSO altogether. The map shows the lean of the longer record.
links.evidence_note: Statistical analysis and ray tracing of the short satellite record link wintertime central-Pacific ENSO conditions to Rossby waves reaching the plateau and to increased winter snowfall; station snow depth and model experiments show positive ENSO deepening early-winter snow over the eastern plateau through suppressed western-Pacific convection, with more snowfall doing more than cold; against it, the ENSO–spring snow cover correlation was significantly positive in 1988–2003 and clearly negative in 2004–19, with some studies finding no relationship.

links.mechanism: A positive dipole means heavy rain over the warm western Indian Ocean in autumn. That rain sends a wave northeastward through the atmosphere that sets up a cyclonic swirl over the central and western plateau in early winter, drawing moisture in from the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal and lifting it into snow.
links.caveat: Two recent studies of a short record, and a dipole usually comes with an El Niño, so the two are hard to separate: one study finds the dipole matters most on the central and western plateau and ENSO on the east, the other finds the dipole's effect holds even with a neutral Pacific. The dipole fades by December, so the snow it adds is early-winter snow, and what happens to the snowpack after that is up to the winter.
links.evidence_note: Station snow depth and model simulations show a positive dipole inducing an anomalous cyclonic circulation over the central western plateau in early winter, transporting extra moisture from the tropics for more snowfall; a positive dipole with either a positive or a neutral ENSO excites the southern Eurasia pattern whose cyclone around the plateau, with enhanced southwesterlies over the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal, brings heavy November–December snowfall in observations and in CAM5 experiments.

links.mechanism: Planetary-scale waves rising from the winter troposphere are steered by the winds they meet in the stratosphere. With easterly wind over the equator the waves cannot cross into the tropics, more of them break against the polar vortex, and the vortex weakens and warms, sometimes suddenly. A weak vortex leaks down through the lower stratosphere over a few weeks and shows at the surface as a negative North Atlantic Oscillation: a weaker Iceland low, a weaker Azores high, and Atlantic westerlies that are slack and pushed south.
links.caveat: An average over many winters, not a rule for one. The effect is clearest in early winter, was nearly absent from 1978 to 1997, and models make it weaker than the record does; a multi-century model run calls the QBO's link to the Arctic Oscillation likely real and its link to the NAO probable but not certain, which is why the arrow is dashed. Which height of the wind matters most is still argued. A chosen NAO is never pushed, so pick the QBO alone with the chain on to see this arrow; the NAO's own winter map then follows one tier down.
links.evidence_note: In sixteen winters of 50 hPa data the high-latitude stratosphere is significantly lower in pressure, a stronger vortex, in westerly than easterly phases, with the largest planetary wave 40% stronger in November–December of easterly phases (Holton and Tan 1980); a review of three decades of work confirms the vortex is weaker in easterly winters while leaving the mechanism and the best height open (Anstey and Shepherd 2014); the easterly phase favours more extreme cold events in northern Europe and eastern North America, with a signature roughly comparable to ENSO's (Thompson, Baldwin and Wallace 2002); weak-vortex events are followed over about two months by negative Arctic Oscillation patterns at the surface (Baldwin and Dunkerton 2001); seasonal hindcasts started on 1 December reproduce a surface Arctic Oscillation response to the QBO (Marshall and Scaife 2009); the January sea-level-pressure response resembles the positive NAO under westerly winds and comes mainly through the polar vortex (Gray et al. 2018); a multi-century model run finds the QBO–Arctic Oscillation link likely real and the QBO–NAO link probable, though weaker than observed (Andrews et al. 2019); the effect faded in 1978–1997 (Lu et al. 2014); the mechanism is argued between the critical-line and meridional- circulation explanations (Garfinkel et al. 2012; Watson and Gray 2014); most models underestimate the early-winter warming of the vortex in easterly phases (Rao et al. 2020); the QBO and ENSO signals in the Arctic stratosphere were correlated in time in the first half of the record and are hard to separate (Garfinkel and Hartmann 2007).

links.mechanism: With westerly wind over the equator, planetary-scale waves rising from the winter troposphere can spread into the tropics, fewer of them break against the polar vortex, and the vortex stays strong and cold. A strong vortex reaches the surface over the following weeks as a positive North Atlantic Oscillation: a deeper Iceland low, a stronger Azores high, and Atlantic westerlies that are stronger and further north.
links.caveat: The same average, with the same doubts, as the easterly side: clearest in early winter, nearly absent from 1978 to 1997, weaker in models than in the record, and probable rather than certain for the NAO itself. Holton and Tan's own late-winter signal did not survive a longer record. A chosen NAO is never pushed, so pick the QBO alone with the chain on to see this arrow.
links.evidence_note: The high-latitude stratosphere is significantly lower in pressure, a stronger vortex, in westerly phases in every month composited (Holton and Tan 1980); the vortex is stronger in westerly winters across the reviewed record (Anstey and Shepherd 2014); the January sea-level-pressure response under westerly winds resembles the positive NAO and is insensitive to the exact height of the westerlies between 10 and 70 hPa (Gray et al. 2018); a surface Arctic Oscillation response appears in hindcasts started on 1 December (Marshall and Scaife 2009); a multi-century model run rates the link to the NAO probable but not certain, and finds it stronger when the westerlies fill a deep layer (Andrews et al. 2019); the effect faded in 1978–1997 (Lu et al. 2014); Arctic stratospheric temperatures in late autumn and early winter are colder in westerly phases (Garfinkel and Hartmann 2007); strengthenings of the vortex are followed by the opposite of the cold-event pattern at the surface (Thompson, Baldwin and Wallace 2002).

links.mechanism: The proposal from the 1980s: in westerly seasons the wind in the lowest stratosphere over the tropical Atlantic is closer to the wind just beneath it, so the tops of growing storms are sheared less and more of them reach hurricane strength. The same seasonal forecasts that first used El Niño also used the QBO.
links.caveat: A link that stopped working, kept on the map as a lesson. From the 1950s to the 1980s westerly seasons were clearly busier and the QBO went into the first seasonal hurricane forecasts; after about 1990 the relationship vanished from the record, and the explanations tried, El Niño, volcanoes, the QBO's own decadal changes, the solar cycle, do not account for it. Drawn dotted for that reason, and read the year: the arrow describes the Atlantic of 1950–1990.
links.evidence_note: Seasonal hurricane frequency in 1950–1982 was substantially above normal when the 30 hPa equatorial wind blew from the west or was turning westerly during the season (Gray 1984); the 30 hPa wind explains about 30% of the variance in August–October Atlantic storm activity in 1955–1983, resilient to removing El Niño years (Shapiro 1989); the relationship is statistically significant from the 1950s to the 1980s and no longer present in later years, with no satisfying explanation found (Camargo and Sobel 2010); a major review lists a possible effect on Atlantic hurricane strength among the QBO's influences (Baldwin et al. 2001).

links.mechanism: The proposal from the 1980s, in reverse: in easterly seasons the wind in the lowest stratosphere over the tropical Atlantic differs more from the wind just beneath it, the tops of growing storms are sheared more, and fewer reach hurricane strength.
links.caveat: The same link that stopped working. Easterly seasons were quieter from the 1950s to the 1980s and not since about 1990; the 2010 season, easterly at the height the map reads until late summer, was one of the busiest on record. Drawn dotted for that reason.
links.evidence_note: Hurricane activity in 1950–1982 was below normal when the 30 hPa equatorial wind blew from the east or was turning easterly during the season (Gray 1984); the in-phase relation with the 50 hPa wind and the 30% of variance explained apply to both phases (Shapiro 1989); the relationship is significant from the 1950s to the 1980s and absent in later years (Camargo and Sobel 2010).

links.mechanism: Where the autumn ice is missing, the open sea heats and moistens the air above it. The warmed air builds a ridge of high pressure over the Urals and the Siberian coast, the ridge steers the storms that would otherwise cross the Barents Sea away, and on its eastern side the Siberian high grows stronger and spreads. Arctic air then drains south across central Siberia: a warm Arctic and a cold continent in the same month. A second path runs through the stratosphere: the ridge sends more wave energy upward, the polar vortex weakens, and the cold deepens over Siberia in late winter.
links.caveat: The most argued arrow on the map. The claim rests on some forty winters, in which low ice and cold Siberia did tend to come together; one large model experiment found the odds of a severe Siberian winter more than doubled by the ice loss, and another traced a stratospheric path. But cold Siberian winters and open Barents water can be two results of the same weather pattern, and when six models were run with and without the observed ice loss the continent did not cool; a twenty-five-winter cooling trend across Eurasia was judged unlikely to be the ice's doing; the ridge over the Urals may cause the low ice rather than follow from it; and a warm Gulf Stream can produce both at once. Dotted for all of that. Read the Siberian card either way: if the link is real it is small in any one winter and the rest is chance.
links.evidence_note: Reduced Barents–Kara ice in a general circulation model produces a high over the polar ocean and easterly flow across the continents, a winter cooling reaching −1.5°C with cold extremes three times more likely (Petoukhov and Semenov 2010); low autumn ice is followed by cold over the Far East in early winter and from Europe to the Far East in late winter, through a stronger Siberian high (Honda, Inoue and Yamane 2009); in light-ice years cyclones stall over the Barents Sea and an anticyclone forms along the Siberian coast, the warm-Arctic cold-Siberian pattern (Inoue, Hori and Takaya 2012); a large ensemble finds the probability of severe winters in central Eurasia more than doubled by the sea-ice decline, through more frequent Eurasian blocking (Mori et al. 2014); a stratospheric pathway links Barents–Kara ice loss to a colder Siberia (Zhang et al. 2018); a cooling trend across Eurasia is linked to the ice (Outten and Esau 2011); reviews of the case for and against (Cohen et al. 2014; Vihma 2014; Overland et al. 2015). Against: twenty-five winters of Eurasian cooling are unlikely to be due to Arctic sea-ice loss (McCusker, Fyfe and Sigmond 2016); neither ice loss nor greenhouse forcing yields colder continents in multiple models, and ice loss reduces cold extremes (Sun, Perlwitz and Hoerling 2016); six coordinated models find the ice changes do not lead to colder Siberian winters (Ogawa et al. 2018); the coincidence of low ice and cold winters is explained by the circulation driving both, with minimal influence from the ice (Blackport et al. 2019), though the modelled cooling may be too weak (Screen and Blackport 2019); a poleward shift of the Gulf Stream front can drive both the ice retreat and the Eurasian cold (Sato, Inoue and Watanabe 2014); Ural blocking in November drives the early-winter response while perturbed ice and snow alone do not (Peings 2019); observed statistics overestimate the causal effect of ice on mid-latitude winters (Blackport and Screen 2021); ice loss alone has played a secondary role relative to natural variability (Overland et al. 2021).

links.mechanism: The ridge that low ice builds over the Urals lines up with the planetary-scale waves of early winter and strengthens them, so more wave energy rises into the stratosphere and breaks against the polar vortex. The vortex weakens and warms, sometimes suddenly, and over the following weeks the weakening leaks back down to the surface as a negative North Atlantic Oscillation: a weaker Iceland low, a weaker Azores high, slack westerlies, cold in northern Europe and the eastern United States, mild in Greenland. The path takes time, which is why the studies find the surface signal in late winter.
links.caveat: Contested, and dotted. The path through the stratosphere is detectable in the record and reproduced by some models, but it appears in only a minority of resampled records, the lagged correlation between autumn ice and the winter NAO has come and gone over the last century, and a model forced with the observed ice alone does not reproduce the relationship, which can instead be generated by the atmosphere's own variability and by the tropics. Sixteen models agree on a weak push toward the negative NAO, worth about a tenth of the swing in any single winter. A chosen NAO is never pushed, so pick the ice alone with the chain on to see this arrow; the NAO's own winter map then follows, still dotted.
links.evidence_note: Barents–Kara sea-ice loss weakens the stratospheric polar vortex in observations and model experiments (Kim et al. 2014); reduced November ice leads to more negative Arctic Oscillation and NAO in early and late winter, with large negative events more than twice as frequent in a high-top model (Nakamura et al. 2015); in a nine- region experiment only Barents–Kara ice loss weakens the vortex and is followed by an NAO-like surface response (Screen 2017); the stratospheric pathway from late-autumn ice to the February NAO is detectable and explains about 26% of its variance but is highly intermittent, appearing in 16% of resampled records (Siew et al. 2020); causal-network analysis finds Barents–Kara ice an important driver of the winter Arctic Oscillation (Kretschmer et al. 2016); models forced by ice loss give a weak negative-NAO response in early winter, often masked by internal variability (Screen et al. 2013; Deser et al. 2010). Against: the observed ice–NAO relationship is reproduced by internal variability and not as a forced response to the ice, with tropical rainfall driving the covariability (Warner, Screen and Scaife 2020); the lagged correlation is non-stationary across centennial reanalyses and large ensembles, which questions its causality (Kolstad and Screen 2019); coupled models capture the delayed ice–vortex–NAO connection but weaker than observed, and its sign varies between ensemble members (Blackport and Screen 2021); sixteen models simulate a robust but weak weakening of the westerlies, an NAO response accounting for around 10% of variations in individual years, and the observed relationship has weakened recently (Smith et al. 2022); models agree in sign but disagree in size (Screen et al. 2018).

links.mechanism: The stronger Siberian high that follows low Barents–Kara ice drives the East Asian winter monsoon: cold air pours south-east out of Siberia across Mongolia and northern China to Korea and Japan. A wave train set off by the heating over the open Arctic water arcs east along the Siberian coast and arrives over East Asia in early winter with high pressure behind it.
links.caveat: Contested. The East Asian link is the best-attested regionally: two studies from different groups found the early-winter cold over the Far East, and one separated it from a different, Pacific-side ice loss that reaches North America. But the same objections apply as for Siberia: the record is short, the statistics can run the other way, and models mostly do not reproduce a cooling. East Asia's winter also answers to ENSO on this map, at a higher tier; when both are chosen the arrows may argue.
links.evidence_note: Significant cold anomalies over the Far East in early winter follow low autumn Arctic ice, reproduced in a model as a stationary wave from the Barents–Kara heating that amplifies the Siberian high (Honda, Inoue and Yamane 2009); warming over the Barents–Kara seas favours cold winters over East Asia while warming over the East Siberian–Chukchi seas favours cold over North America (Kug et al. 2015); the winter Siberian high is stronger after low autumn ice in the eastern Arctic and Siberian marginal seas, with September ice a precursor beyond what tropical seas predict (Wu, Su and Zhang 2011); light-ice years bring an anticyclone along the Siberian coast and cold advection over eastern Siberia (Inoue, Hori and Takaya 2012); early-winter reduced Barents–Kara ice may reinforce existing teleconnections to central Asia and downstream East Asia (Overland et al. 2021); reviews of the East Asian case (Gao et al. 2014; Vihma 2014). Against: multi-model experiments give no cooling of the continents from ice loss (Sun, Perlwitz and Hoerling 2016; Ogawa et al. 2018); the coincidence is explained by the circulation driving both (Blackport et al. 2019); ice loss alone has played a secondary role (Overland et al. 2021).

links.mechanism: The ridge over the Urals that follows low ice blocks the mild Atlantic air that usually crosses European Russia in winter, and on its western flank Arctic air from the Barents and Kara coasts is steered south over the Russian plain. The first model study of the link put the largest cooling here, over Europe and northern Asia, and named the cold winter of 2005–06 as its example.
links.caveat: Contested, and read with the Siberian arrow: the same studies for, the same studies against. Western Russia's winter also answers to the North Atlantic Oscillation on this map at the established tier, and the ice pushes the NAO the same way, so with the chain on this region can be cold twice over from one cause. A twenty-five-winter cooling trend across Eurasia, the strongest evidence for this arrow in the 2010s, has since been judged more likely chance than ice.
links.evidence_note: Lower Barents–Kara ice concentration in a model brings a continental-scale winter cooling reaching −1.5°C, with cold extremes over large areas including Europe more than three times as likely, in a non-linear response that peaks at intermediate ice loss (Petoukhov and Semenov 2010); zonally elongated cold anomalies from Europe to the Far East in late winter follow low ice, with the negative NAO (Honda, Inoue and Yamane 2009); the odds of severe winters in central Eurasia more than doubled (Mori et al. 2014); a cooling trend over Eurasia is linked to the ice (Outten and Esau 2011); the recent ice reduction results in cold winters in mid- latitude continental regions in a high-top model (Nakamura et al. 2015). Against: the Eurasian cooling of 1990–2015 is unlikely due to ice loss (McCusker, Fyfe and Sigmond 2016); no cooling in multi- model experiments (Sun, Perlwitz and Hoerling 2016; Ogawa et al. 2018); minimal influence of the ice on coincident cold winters (Blackport et al. 2019); the statistics are inflated by the circulation's effect on the ice (Blackport and Screen 2021).

links.mechanism: Snow cools the ground beneath it, so a wide October snow cover builds the Siberian high early and strong. The high sits where the planetary-scale waves of early winter have their source, and it strengthens them, so more wave energy rises into the stratosphere in November and December and breaks against the polar vortex. The vortex weakens and warms, and over the following weeks the weakening works its way down to the surface as the negative phase of the Arctic Oscillation, which on this map is the negative NAO: high pressure over the pole, slack westerlies, cold spilling south. Six steps, each of them observed in 2009–10.
links.caveat: Contested, and dotted. The correlation was found in the satellite era, from 1972, and a reanalysis of the whole twentieth century shows it did not exist before the 1970s; it may depend on the phase of the equatorial stratospheric wind, or be a statistical accident. Models give a weak version at best, and some suggest the autumn circulation makes the snow rather than the snow making the winter. Since about 2010 the forecasts that used it have missed badly. The satellite snow record itself charted more October snow after 1990 than other data show. A chosen NAO is never pushed, so pick the snow alone with the chain on to see this arrow; the NAO's own winter map then follows, still dotted. The Barents–Kara ice pushes the NAO the same way, and the two precursors are largely one signal; picking both is not evidence that they add up.
links.evidence_note: Early-season Eurasian snow cover is associated with a stronger, more expansive Siberian high and with the dominant mode of winter variability in the following winter (Cohen and Entekhabi 1999); the correlation between autumn snow and winter circulation strengthens downward from the stratosphere, consistent with snow acting through upward-propagating waves (Saito, Cohen and Entekhabi 2001); a model forced with the highest (1976) and lowest (1988) observed Siberian snow produces a downward-propagating negative Arctic Oscillation through the winter (Gong, Entekhabi and Cohen 2003); years with large October snow feature strong upward wave pulses, a weaker vortex and high polar heights (Cohen et al. 2007); a hundred-member ensemble reproduces the stratosphere–troposphere response to a Siberian snow anomaly (Fletcher et al. 2009); prescribing observed snow in a model that lacked it recovers the snow–AO relationship and the recent AO trend (Allen and Zender 2011); a snow-advance index explains a large fraction of the winter AO's variance (Cohen and Jones 2011); in high-snow years surface pressure is higher from 1 November and the lower-stratospheric heat flux is stronger from mid-November, with surface-to-stratosphere wave events nearly twice as frequent (Cohen et al. 2014); the snow–NAO link is strongest in Arctic warming periods, for November snow (Wegmann et al. 2020). Against: the teleconnection is not stationary and did not emerge until the 1970s, with the QBO a possible modulator, so statistical forecasts should not rest on snow alone (Peings et al. 2013); the snow–AO relationship has only emerged since the 1970s, the QBO modulation may be a purely stochastic effect, and empirical prediction from snow or ice alone is limited (Douville, Peings and Saint-Martin 2017); CMIP5 models do not capture a robust link (Furtado et al. 2015); the remote influence of snow is weak in two models, the atmosphere may have driven the snow rather than the reverse, and the teleconnection may be a stochastic artefact (Peings et al. 2017); snow–atmosphere coupling is real locally but the remote link is weak in models and non-stationary in the record (Henderson et al. 2018); causal analysis finds snow's role on the AO unclear (Kretschmer et al. 2016); only November snow, not October, covaries significantly with the winter NAO (Santolaria- Otín et al. 2020); the November snow dipole and Barents–Kara ice are driven by the same Scandinavian pattern (Gastineau, García- Serrano and Frankignoul 2017); the rising October snow trend in the NOAA charts is an internal artefact of the dataset (Brown and Derksen 2013).

links.mechanism: The same path, one step further: the weakened vortex and the negative Arctic Oscillation that follow a snowy Siberian October put a blocking high over Greenland and the pole, and Arctic air is steered south down the eastern side of North America, where the big coastal snowstorms follow. The index's makers found their snow index a better guide to eastern United States winter temperature than the observed winter AO itself.
links.caveat: Contested, and the arrow with the most public record of failure. In October 2016 the snow spread across Siberia wider than in all but a handful of Octobers, and the forecasts built on it called for a cold, snowy winter in the eastern United States; the winter was the sixth warmest in the American record and February 2017 the second warmest. The link is drawn for the winters it fitted, 1976–77 and 2009–10 above all. The eastern United States is also reached by the NAO's own arrow on this map, at the established tier; with the chain on this region carries two arrows from one cause.
links.evidence_note: A snow index built from summer and autumn anomalies is more highly correlated with eastern United States winter temperatures than the observed winter AO (Cohen and Saito 2003); a statistical forecast model using October snow and pressure shows positive skill over the eastern United States in seven real-time winters and thirty-three hindcasts, where dynamical models had none (Cohen and Fletcher 2007); a model forced with the snow of the winter of 1977–78 reproduces the observed mid-latitude circulation anomalies (Cohen and Entekhabi 2001); in 2009–10 the expansion of cold into the eastern United States followed the second stratospheric warming and Mid-Atlantic snowfalls exceeded 135 cm in seventeen days (Cohen et al. 2010). Against: the snow–AO teleconnection did not exist before the 1970s (Peings et al. 2013; Douville, Peings and Saint- Martin 2017) and may be a stochastic artefact (Peings et al. 2017); the winter of 2016–17 was the sixth warmest on record for the contiguous United States after a wide October snow (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information 2017; Rutgers Global Snow Lab); the severe winter of 1976–77 has been attributed instead to the Pacific and a persistent El Niño (Namias 1978).

links.mechanism: Two paths into Europe. Directly, the early, strong Siberian high pushes cold air west across Russia toward Scandinavia and Germany. Through the stratosphere, the weakened vortex and the negative Arctic Oscillation that follow slacken the Atlantic westerlies, so the mild maritime air stops at the coast and northern Europe sits under Arctic or continental air for weeks at a time, as it did in the winter of 2009–10.
links.caveat: Contested. The statistical model that used October snow had skill over northern Eurasia in hindcasts, and the winter of 2009–10 fits the path step by step; but the same twentieth-century reanalysis that undercuts the NAO link undercuts this one, and the winter of 2019–20, after a wide October snow, was the mildest on record across much of Europe with the strongest polar vortex and the most positive Arctic Oscillation ever measured. Northern Europe is also reached by the NAO's own arrow at the established tier; with the chain on this region carries two arrows from one cause.
links.evidence_note: The snow-based forecast model has positive skill over northern Eurasia in hindcasts and real-time forecasts (Cohen and Fletcher 2007); the cooling effect of snow builds a stronger, more expansive Siberian high with more frequent intrusions west (Cohen and Entekhabi 1999); winter cooling trends across northern Eurasia in the last two decades are argued to follow increasing autumn snow (Cohen et al. 2012); in 2009–10 the cold that reached Europe followed the two stratospheric warmings (Cohen et al. 2010). Against: the teleconnection is non-stationary (Peings et al. 2013; Douville, Peings and Saint-Martin 2017); weak or absent in models (Furtado et al. 2015; Henderson et al. 2018); the increasing snow trend behind the cooling argument is largely a dataset artefact (Brown and Derksen 2013); the winter of 2019–20 featured an exceptionally strong vortex and an unprecedentedly positive Arctic Oscillation with above-normal temperatures across Europe (Lawrence et al. 2020) after an above-normal October snow (Rutgers Global Snow Lab).

NOAA Climate Prediction Center. Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), ERSST version 6: the three-month running mean of the Niño-3.4 sea-surface temperature anomaly, 1950 to date. Read for the years table in August 2026 with NOAA's own rule: an El Niño or La Niña is called when the index stays at or beyond +0.5 °C or −0.5 °C for at least five overlapping seasons; the onset is the centre month of the first such season and the duration counts the seasons.

NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Dipole Mode Index from HadISST 1.1 (the Saji et al. 1999 boxes, 10°S–10°N, 50–70°E minus 10°S–0°, 90–110°E), monthly, 1870 to date. Read for the years table in August 2026: a positive or negative dipole is called when the three-month running mean stays at or beyond +0.35 °C or −0.35 °C for at least two overlapping seasons touching June–November, the dipole's own season. The threshold sits a little under the Bureau of Meteorology's ±0.4 because this monthly HadISST index runs smaller than the Bureau's weekly one; with it the Bureau's list of dipole years since 1980 is reproduced except the weak negative events of 2014 and 2021.

NOAA Climate Prediction Center. North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) index, monthly, standardised, 1950 to date. Read for the years table in August 2026: a winter is positive when its December–February mean is at or above +0.5 and negative at or below −0.5, in standardised units; the phase is dated from December and held three months.

British Antarctic Survey. Station-based Southern Annular Mode index (Marshall 2003), monthly, 1957 to date. Read for the years table in August 2026: a positive or negative SAM is called when the three-month running mean stays at or beyond +1.5 or −1.5 (the index's standard deviation is about 1.2) for at least two overlapping seasons; the year's entry is the first such run to begin in the year, and the others are named in its note.

NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Pacific Decadal Oscillation index from ERSST version 5, monthly, 1854 to date. Read for the years table in August 2026: a year is positive when its calendar-year mean is at or above +0.5 and negative at or below −0.5; a run of same-phase years is one phase, dated from January of its first year.

NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation index, unsmoothed and detrended, from the Kaplan SST version 2 North Atlantic mean, monthly, 1856 to January 2023. Read for the years table in August 2026, for 1980–2022: a year is positive when its calendar-year mean is at or above +0.1 °C and negative at or below −0.1 °C; a run of same-phase years is one phase, dated from January of its first year.

NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. North Atlantic (0–60°N) sea-surface temperature anomaly from ERSST version 5, monthly, 1854 to date, offered as an AMO index. Read for the years table in August 2026, for 2023 onwards, where the Kaplan series ends: its calendar-year means were linearly detrended over 1854–2025 for this table and read with the same ±0.1 °C rule. Over 1980–2022 the two series give the same phase in most years and differ in eight, all with the Kaplan value within 0.07 °C of the threshold.

NOAA ERSST version 5, Atlantic Niño (ATL3) index computed for the years table in August 2026. Sea-surface temperature averaged over 3°S–3°N, 20°W–0° from the monthly ERSST v5 grid (Huang and others, 2017), as anomalies from the 1991–2020 monthly means; a warm or cool event is called when the three-month running mean is at or beyond +0.5 °C or −0.5 °C, about one standard deviation, for at least one season, the rule the Atlantic Niño literature uses; the year's entry is the first such event to begin in the year.

NOAA ERSST version 5, Indian Ocean Basin Mode index computed for the years table in September 2026. Sea-surface temperature averaged over 20°S–20°N, 40–110°E from the monthly ERSST v5 grid (Huang and others, 2017), as anomalies from the 1991–2020 monthly means with the linear trend over 1980–2025 (+0.14 °C a decade) removed, since the mode is the year-to-year swing on top of the basin's warming; a warm or cool basin is called when the three-month running mean is at or beyond +0.25 °C or −0.25 °C, about one standard deviation, for at least two overlapping seasons; the year's entry is the first such event to begin in the year.

NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Atlantic Meridional Mode (AMM) sea-surface temperature index of Chiang and Vimont (2004), monthly, January 1948 to August 2024, where the series ends. Read for the years table in September 2026: a positive or negative AMM is called when the three-month running mean is at or beyond +2.5 or −2.5, about one standard deviation, for at least two overlapping seasons; the year's entry is the first such event to begin in the year, and 2025 is not recorded.

NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Pacific Meridional Mode (PMM) sea-surface temperature index of Chiang and Vimont (2004), monthly, January 1948 to August 2024, where the series ends. Read for the years table in September 2026: a positive or negative PMM is called when the three-month running mean is at or beyond +3 or −3, about one standard deviation, for at least two overlapping seasons; the year's entry is the first such event to begin in the year, and 2025 is not recorded.

NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies. Stratospheric aerosol optical depth at 550 nm by latitude, monthly, 1979 to 2025, derived by A. Lacis from the Global Space-based Stratospheric Aerosol Climatology version 2.24 (Kovilakam and others, 2020). Read for the years table in September 2026 as the area-weighted global mean: an eruption is in force while the monthly value is above 0.02, about four times the quiet background of 0.005; the onset is the first such month and the duration counts the months above it. Only El Chichón (1982) and Pinatubo (1991) qualify in these years; the Hunga Tonga eruption of January 2022 lifted the value to 0.015 at most and is not called.

NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Quasi-Biennial Oscillation index: monthly mean zonal wind at 30 hPa over the equator from the NCEP/NCAR reanalysis, 1948 to date, in m/s. Read for the years table in September 2026: the phase is the sign of the monthly wind, westerly or easterly, beginning in the first month of the new sign and holding until the next change; a reversal shorter than three months is ignored; the year's entry is the first phase to begin in the year, the other named in its note. Checked against the Singapore radiosonde series of the Freie Universität Berlin at the same level for 1990–2021: the two agree on every phase change to within three months, except that the balloons show the weak easterly interruption of early 2020 as two months only, under this rule's three; the disruption of February 2016 cut through the westerlies at 40 hPa, one level lower, and shows at 30 hPa only as a weakening.

National Snow and Ice Data Center. Sea Ice Index, version 4 (Fetterer and others), regional monthly extent for the Barents and Kara seas, November 1978 to date. Read for the years table in September 2026 as the October–November mean of the two seas together, with the linear trend over 1979–2025 (−0.18 million km² a decade) removed, since the links describe the year-to-year swing rather than the long decline: high or low ice is called when the departure from the trend line is at or beyond +0.2 or −0.2 million km², about one standard deviation; the phase is dated from October and held six months, to March, the winter the links describe.

Rutgers University Global Snow Lab (Robinson, D. A.). Eurasia monthly snow cover extent from the NOAA climate data record, November 1966 to date. Read for the years table in September 2026 as the October extent against the 1991–2020 October mean of 10.7 million km², with the linear trend over 1980–2025 (+0.9 million km² a decade, disputed as an artefact of the record's change of method by Brown and Derksen 2013) removed: high or low snow is called when the departure from the trend line is at or beyond +1.5 or −1.5 million km², about one standard deviation; the phase is dated from October and held six months, to March, the winter the links describe. This is the month's extent, not the rate of advance across it that the snow-advance index of Cohen and Jones (2011) reads.
